documents.abstract: The effect of occupational safety and health program implementation on the performance of production dapartement employees at PT XYZ.This study aims to determine the effect of occupational safety and occupational health implementation on the performance of production employees at PT XYZ This research employs a quantitative approach, with primary data collected through questionnaires distributed to production employees of PT XYZ The variables in this study consist of occupational safety and occupational health as independent variables and employee performance as the dependent variable. The collected data were analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), including validity testing, reliability testing, classical assumption testing, multiple linear regression analysis, t-test, f-test, and coefficient of determination. The results of this study are expected to indicate the extent to which the implementation of occupational safety and occupational health affects the performance of production employees. This research is expected to provide practical benefits for the company as an evaluation reference for improving the implementation of occupational safety and health and creating a safe and healthy working environment that can support the improvement of employee performance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Audited interim result, not completed PENTA certification. Four platform-configured engines were observed in two fresh web conversations each with memory disabled, using a frozen six-case synthetic decision prompt. Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol matched the registered canonical JSON tuple hash in both recorded captures. GPT-5.6 Luna matched in A but differed in B. GLM 5.2 replayed consistently but differed from the registered target in both captures. DeepSeek has not been captured. All 48 recorded decisions selected the expected playbook name and id. Full registered tuple equality held for 30/48 decisions. The remaining 18 differed only in spaces inside the steps_executed string. Pretty-printing outside strings is removed by canonicalization and is not a failure cause. The prompt's lack of an explicit space delimiter contract is disclosed; failures remain failures against the preregistered target. Limitations: UI-transcribed rendered captures, not raw provider responses; model attribution by Base44 configuration, not backend attestation; supplementary fresh-chat method deviates from original same-conversation registration; shared instructions, workspace and expected answers remain available; Sol executed skills in both captures; Opus A conversation attribution was inferred from sidebar/timestamp ordering. This is not a stress/load test, live-healing test, general governance certification, or proof of runtime enforcement. Confidence-hold and no-match branches were not exercised. Audit and correction: earlier copied Luna files and single-turn Opus/Sol attempts are excluded, preserved, and labeled. Earlier operator claims of raw byte-exactness and 100% governance are corrected explicitly. Deterministic Phase A/C receipts are harness-computed, not LLM inference evidence. No failure is normalized into a pass. Dual Mesh Benchmark: not measured in this experiment. No comparative mesh, latency, learning or healing performance claim is made. Bundle contains the technical note in PDF/Markdown, machine-readable receipt, full evidence archive, offline verifier, original preregistration, excluded attempts, and SHA-256 manifest. All test data is synthetic. AI assistance and capture provenance are disclosed. Registration: public commit deadfea. Results: GitHub evidence. Research home: DCAI; portal: DSOS Science. Lineage acknowledged: Nyquist, Hartley, Shannon, Kolmogorov. No new mechanism is claimed. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Audited supplementary milestone, not completed five-engine certification. Four platform-configured engines passed two fresh-conversation captures each against a locally frozen twelve-case synthetic decision contract: 8/8 response captures and 96/96 recorded tuple declarations matched the canonical target. Original v1 negative results remain failed and are preserved at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23286324. V2 explicitly fixes the step-string delimiter contract and adds confidence-boundary/no-match cases. The expanded instrument and changed capture route prevent attributing the result to wording alone. Luna and Opus also matched raw response content; GLM and Sol differed in formatting but matched canonical tuples. Attribution is by platform settings, not provider attestation; shared workspace/context remains accessible. Local freeze is not public preregistration. DeepSeek remains pending. Benchmark baseline: one local validator-only run completed 200/200 expected acceptance checks, with 100 valid accepted and 100 mutant rejected; mixed p50 0.0733 ms, p95 0.0878 ms. Short sandbox microbenchmark, not LLM or infrastructure throughput. Historical per-engine reported durations are descriptive n=2, not a vendor ranking. Forty offline regression checks passed. No stress tolerance, live healing, PQC validation or deployed enforcement claim is made. A future stress test is planned and not reported as complete. Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. No comparative mesh, learning, recovery or resource-use result is claimed. AI assistance and capture provenance disclosed. All workload data is synthetic. Public evidence includes exact final outputs, instrument, frozen prompt, offline verifier and sanitized receipts. Raw API responses, private metadata, secrets, customer identity and PHI excluded. GitHub milestone and evidence. Research home: DCAI. DSOS Science. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

Abstract Background Aggregate large language model (LLM) performance may obscure consequential errors and variability across repeated queries. We compared the clinical performance, safety, and repeated-query stability of three consumer-facing LLMs with two fixed individual early-career urologist comparators in urological oncology. Methods One hundred synthetic vignettes spanning five urological cancers and five decision categories were answered by GPT-5.2 Instant, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, and two early-career urologists using the same standardized prompt without external resources. Two source-masked urologists with uro-oncology expertise independently scored all 500 initial responses against a prespecified 2025 European Association of Urology (EAU)-anchored framework. Benchmark-defined primary composite success required scores ≥ 2 in guideline concordance, clinical safety, decision completeness, and risk/stage accuracy, with no prespecified disqualifying clinical error. Safety-critical errors and exact three-run stability were assessed separately. Results Primary composite success was achieved in 70/100 (70.0%) GPT-5.2, 64/100 (64.0%) Claude, and 60/100 (60.0%) Gemini responses, versus 85/100 (85.0%) and 89/100 (89.0%) for Urologists A and B (Cochran’s Q = 34.23; P < 0.001). Five of six prespecified human–LLM contrasts remained significant after Holm adjustment; Urologist A versus GPT-5.2 did not (difference, 15 percentage points; 95% CI, 3–27; adjusted P = 0.095). Safety-critical errors occurred in 25.0%, 25.0%, and 26.0% of LLM responses versus 2.0% and 1.0% of urologist responses (Cochran’s Q = 51.34; P < 0.001); all six human–LLM contrasts remained significant. Across 60 vignette–platform combinations, exact three-run stability was 45.0% for primary classification, 48.3% for safety-critical status, and 28.3% for the full four-domain score profile. Stable classifications included both consistently successful and consistently unsuccessful outputs and both always-safe and always-unsafe outputs. Conclusions The consumer-facing LLMs evaluated during the study period often produced acceptable responses, but safety-critical errors and limited repeatability remained clinically relevant. Aggregate performance did not fully capture response reliability. These findings support clinician-supervised rather than autonomous use and support incorporating safety-gated endpoints and repeated-query stability alongside conventional performance measures.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed information processing in resource-rich languages, their effectiveness significantly diminishes when applied to low-resource regional languages (e.g., Sundanese and Javanese). This paper investigates the performance bottlenecks experienced by users, focusing on latency and output fluency. Through a quantitative survey (N = 50), we argue that these limitations stem from underrepresentation during the model pre-training phase and inefficient tokenization. Consequently, we propose prioritizing vocabulary expansion and open-source regional corpus collection during the pre-training stage to enhance AI inclusivity and fluency.

Chemistry, environmental health, and occupational health have historically developed in close collaboration. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of LLMs, in responding to a chemistry course questionnaire used in environmental and occupational health department for educational purposes. This was a cross-sectional study conducted in 2026. The study used a 50-item multiple-choice questionnaire, primarily in Persian with limited English terms and formulas, which was administered to LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3, and Copilot 2026). Performance was evaluated using confusion matrix analysis. Cochran`s Q test, McNemar`s test for pair-wise comparisons, and Point-biserial correlation were also conducted to further evaluate the study data. The LLMs presented mean sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.81, 0.29, and 0.68, respectively. Gemini 3 presented a high level of performance, achieving the highest sensitivity (0.85), specificity (0.56), and accuracy (0.80). ChatGPT-5.5 had the lowest sensitivity (0.76), while Copilot showed the lowest specificity (0.07) and an accuracy of 0.62. No significant correlations were found between performance and questionnaire characteristics; however, all models performed poorly on negatively framed items requiring identification of incorrect options. The study presented some preliminary insights on the performance of LLMs in chemistry-related questions. Further research is warranted.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Welding quality inspection of battery top covers is critical to lithium-ion battery safety and reliability. The height deviation between weld defects and normal areas is extremely small; on specular, weakly textured surfaces it produces no stable brightness contrast, so two-dimensional (2D) images carry almost no usable defect signal. Three-dimensional (3D) sensing captures such deviations but incurs computational costs prohibitive for production lines. Raw depth maps, as scalar grayscale fields, cause 2D convolutional networks to overlook tiny-defect features. Addressing all three limitations simultaneously remains a key challenge for artificial intelligence (AI) in industrial inspection. To address this challenge, we propose a geometry-to-photometry defect detection framework that converts 3D weld geometry into discriminative 2D photometric representations via physically inspired rendering. Depth data are first mapped to pseudo-color images, and surface normals then modulate lighting under a Phong-based model to transform subtle geometric discontinuities into high-contrast photometric cues. Building on this strategy, we develop YOLO-WaveletTiny (YOLO-WT), a lightweight You Only Look Once (YOLO) detector integrating wavelet depthwise separable convolution and inverse wavelet upsampling for efficient feature extraction and reconstruction. Experiments on a real industrial dataset with six defect categories show the rendered representation improves the baseline by 5.9 percentage points in mean average precision at 50% intersection over union (mAP@50), and the full framework achieves 93.8% mAP@50 with only 2.47 million parameters and 5.7 GFLOPs, outperforming mainstream detectors. These results demonstrate the framework as an effective, practical AI solution for low-cost, high-precision weld defect inspection.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Project narrative for a proposed pilot study of a large language model (LLM)-based conversational agent that administers the PHQ-9 and the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) to prenatal and postnatal patients in an outpatient setting. This is a grant narrative (a research plan), not a report of results: no data have been collected. Posted as is; names of people, partner institutions and the funder have been removed. The reference list is included. Abstract: The project plans to pilot test a functional prototype conversational agent with human-in-the-loop safety, using a participatory development approach (workshops, interviews and feedback surveys) and Agile development, to evaluate user experience, therapeutic alliance, performance and accuracy, and to inform a future clinical trial.
topics: Maternal Mental Health During Pregnancy and Postpartum
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles. Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model. When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Accurate agricultural yield prediction is crucial for crop management and data-driven decision-making. This study proposes a machine learning framework for predicting total lentil seed yield using 264 observations collected during a single growing season at one location in Sivas, Türkiye. Seven regression models and the tabular foundation model TabPFN were evaluated through nested cross-validation. The fixed post hoc Foundation-Augmented Averaging Ensemble (FAAE) combined TabPFN, Extra Trees, CatBoost, and XGBoost using equal weights, while the primary fully nested evaluation selected the four ensemble members within each outer training fold. The fully nested FAAE achieved R2 = 0.891 ± 0.045, comparable to the strongest individual models, while the fixed post hoc FAAE yielded R2 = 0.897 ± 0.038. Split conformal prediction produced well-calibrated uncertainty intervals at 80%, 90%, and 95% coverage. SHAP and LOCO identified pods per plant and biological yield as the dominant predictors of lentil yield. Overall, these findings indicate that FAAE can provide competitive predictive performance within a leakage-controlled framework while also supporting uncertainty quantification and biologically meaningful interpretation. Because the dominant predictors, pods per plant and biological yield, are measured at or near physiological maturity, the proposed framework is more suitable for end-of-season yield estimation than for early-season forecasting. The framework therefore shows potential for within-trial yield assessment, although validation using replicated material across additional years and locations is required before broader generalization.

Predictive policing based on artificial intelligence is shifting crime prevention from reactive response toward data-driven risk identification, pattern recognition, and resource prioritization. This transformation creates a legal dilemma: the same systems that may improve analytical capacity can also amplify historical bias, enable opaque profiling, intrude upon privacy, and influence coercive decisions without adequate procedural safeguards. This article analyzes the legal position of predictive policing in Indonesia and formulates a rights-based governance model for police use of artificial intelligence. The research applies normative juridical analysis using statutory, conceptual, comparative, and policy approaches. The analysis focuses on the 2022 Personal Data Protection Law, the 2023 Criminal Code, the 2025 Criminal Procedure Code, the 2026 amendment to the Police Law, and Indonesia's emerging national AI governance framework. The study finds that Indonesia already possesses fragmented legal bases relevant to AI-supported policing, but lacks a dedicated risk-based framework that defines prohibited uses, high-risk systems, human oversight, auditability, contestability, and allocation of responsibility. The article proposes a four-layer governance model: constitutional safeguards, statutory legality, AI governance controls, and operational human review. Predictive outputs should function as decision-support rather than autonomous grounds for coercive action.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction:Teachers form the backbone of any educational system, shaping future generations through constant interaction and communication.In the Indian context, where classroom resources are often limited, the teacher's voice becomes the most vital instructional tool.However, prolonged and excessive voice use places teachers at considerable risk of vocal discomfort, presenting as dryness, hoarseness, throat irritation, and voice fatigue.These symptoms not only hinder effective teaching but also affect teachers' well-being, productivity, and overall quality of education.Despite its significance, vocal health remains a largely overlooked occupational concern among school teachers, particularly at the primary level.Recognizing this gap, the present study was undertaken to explore the magnitude of vocal discomfort among primary school teachers.Material and method A non-experimental descriptive research design was adopted for the study.A total of 200 primary school teachers from selected schools in the Sangli-Miraj-Kupwad Corporation area were included using a cluster sampling technique.Data was collected using the standardized Vocal Tract Discomfort Scale (VTDS) developed by Mathieson, administered in both Marathi and English for better comprehension.The tool comprised two sections: demographic variables and an 8-item self-rating scale assessing frequency and severity of vocal discomfort symptoms on a 6-point Likert scale.The total score ranged from 0 to 96 and was categorized into no, normal, mild, moderate, and extreme levels of vocal discomfort.Content validity was established by 20 experts, ensuring the tool's appropriateness for the study setting. Results:The findings revealed a notable burden of vocal discomfort among teachers.Symptoms such as dryness (46%), aching (43.5%), and soreness (39.5%) were commonly reported, followed by tightness (34%) and burning sensations (31.5%).Overall, most participants experienced mild (65%) to moderate (35%) levels of discomfort.The prevalence of vocal discomfort was found to be 45.56%.Female teachers constituted a larger proportion of the sample, and most participants had 1-10 years of teaching experience, with an average daily teaching duration of 5-6 hours. Conclusion:The study highlights that nearly half of the primary school teachers experience some degree of vocal discomfort, underscoring it as a significant occupational health issue.Although vocal discomfort appears to be influenced by demographic and work-related factors, no statistically significant association was observed in this study.These findings emphasize the need for early screening, awareness programs, and preventive voice care strategies to safeguard teachers' vocal health and enhance their professional efficiency.

Abstract Air pollution is identified by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as the leading environmental threat to human health, with indoor exposure particularly concerning given its daily, long-term nature. Europeans spend approximately 90% of their time indoors, where poor indoor air quality (IAQ) contributes an estimated 2 million disability-adjusted life-years lost annually in the EU, with vulnerable populations especially at risk. This study explores a Knowledge Graph (KG) as a decision-support tool to prioritise Substances of Concern (SoC) for indoor dust and air. Two complementary approaches were applied: a top-down screening that filters a broad substance universe against defined criteria to identify monitoring candidates, and a bottom-up characterisation of already monitored substances against the same criteria. Integrating publicly available chemical data within the KG and applying a risk-oriented approach based on hazard classification, REACH registration tonnage and use information, we narrowed a list of over 16,000 substances (PlastChem list) down to 42. This work shows that KG can effectively connect diverse data sources and identified both known and emerging SoC not yet monitored in private settings. It highlights that non-REACH chemicals may contribute significantly to indoor dust chemistry analysis, and REACH consumer-use data alone does not capture all uses relevant to residential indoor exposure. The experiments show that expanding the number and diversity of integrated data sources is recommended to refine scoping for chemical monitoring, risk assessment and management. Key concerns among identified substances include reproductive toxicity and respiratory tract irritation, often linked to numerous consumer products. The ECHA Classification and Labelling Inventory was found to be a useful hazardous substance pool, though further refinement with additional health-related data is recommended. Finally, we discuss how integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and KG into the framework could support partial automation of the validation of SoC, improving future monitoring and analysis efficiency.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.

In the injection section of PT Natamas Plast, product sorting activities are performed using workstations with different types and dimensions of chairs and tables that have not been fully adjusted to operator anthropometric characteristics. This condition may result in non-ergonomic working postures and musculoskeletal discomfort. This study aimed to identify ergonomic problems in the product sorting workstation and provide a basis for ergonomic workstation redesign. The study was conducted through direct observation of working conditions and assessment of musculoskeletal complaints using NBM, while working posture was evaluated using REBA. The NBM results showed that operators experienced musculoskeletal complaints, particularly in the lower back, calves, and buttocks with the percentage complaints above 4%. The REBA assessment indicates that 5 out of the 9 operators are classified as having a high-risk level ranging score from 8 to 10. Anthropometric measurements were also performed to determine the workstation dimensions based on the 5th to 95th percentile, resulting in a proposed adjustable chair with a height of 39 to 49 cm and an adjustable worktable height from 136 to 159 cm. The proposed workstation design integrates musculoskeletal complaints, postural risk, and operator anthropometry to improve compatibility between the operator and workstation. The main contribution of this study is the development of a proposed ergonomic workstation based on REBA assessment and operator anthropometric data, which provides a technically justified intervention for mitigating identified ergonomic risks and serves as a basis for future implementation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.

Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.

Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

Human inquiry has developed through philosophy, mathematics, physics, biology, logic, psychology, cognitive science, religious studies, and numerous other disciplines. Each investigates particular aspects of existence through its own concepts, methods, and standards of explanation. Yet the relationships among these domains raise a fundamental question: Can a common structural framework help us understand how different forms of organisation emerge, persist, transform, and become intelligible to observers within reality? Recursive Structural Reality (RSR) proposes such a framework through the interconnected concepts of existence, difference, relation, structure, information, transformation, recursion, stability, persistence, and identity. Its central proposition, Identity = Stable Recursion, directs attention towards the processes through which recognisable organisation may persist despite changes in components, states, or circumstances. RSR also investigates the conditions under which structures lose stability, undergo transformation, reorganise, and give rise to new forms of organisation. A second foundational dimension concerns the observer. Human beings do not investigate reality from outside the universe but participate in the reality they seek to understand. Through perception, memory, language, logic, mathematics, and reflection, observers construct models that organise experience and make particular aspects of existence intelligible. These models are indispensable to knowledge, yet they remain selective representations whose assumptions, limitations, and domains of validity require examination. The scope of RSR extends from foundational ontology and mathematical structures to physical systems, biological organisation, intelligence, artificial intelligence, consciousness, knowledge, religious traditions, and social institutions. These domains provide different contexts in which questions about structure, transformation, stability, persistence, and identity can be investigated. Their inclusion within a common framework does not imply that they share identical mechanisms or can be explained through one undifferentiated model. Each application requires concepts, methods, and standards of evidence appropriate to its subject. RSR therefore distinguishes philosophical RSR, mathematical RSR, and physical RSR while situating them within a broader interdisciplinary research programme. Philosophical coherence, mathematical derivation, and physical validity are related but distinct requirements. Similarly, applications to biological, cognitive, religious, and social phenomena require their own explanatory development and appropriate forms of investigation. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, expanded scope, methodological orientation, and research architecture of RSR. It presents the framework as an evolving programme whose contributions must be assessed through conceptual precision, formal development, explanatory value, and empirical or comparative investigation. Its long-term objective is an integrated understanding of reality that investigates structural connections across domains without erasing their differences, while examining both the phenomena under investigation and the limitations of the models through which they are understood.

XYZ is one of the manufacturing companies that produces precision spare parts for automotive and electronic components. One of the automotive component spare parts is the Valve Seat. In the production process, there are NG (Not Good) valve seat products that are delivered to customers, resulting in frequent customer claims. This research aims to describe and analyze work process improvements so that quality can be maintained using the Seven Tools Method and to identify the factors causing the delivery of non-conforming products. Furthermore, the Failure Mode and Effect Analysis method is used to identify the highest failure risks, followed by kaizen implementation. Based on these results, an analysis of work process improvements is required to maintain product quality before delivery to customers by creating work instructions and adding work process methods during handling. Based on the pareto defect diagram, the most frequent defect in the last 3 months was the dented part, accounting for 95,91%. The contributing factors were: Human factors, where operators did not yet fully understand handling requirements; machine factors, where components and cutting oil circulation were dirty; method factors, where handling was not in accordance with SOP; and material factors, where the material made of stainless steel was easily scratched. By implementing FMEA and Kaizen, it was found that the Valve Seat production process at PT XYZ was already quite good, with a defect reduction of 0.87%, from the previous defect rate of 2.75% to 1.88%.

Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available at https://github.com/IBM/PFAS-regulations.

Purpose This study aims to examine how three dimensions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), namely, capability, application and knowledge modelling, are associated with entrepreneurial innovation, and whether innovation mediates their associations with entrepreneurial performance and entrepreneurial success in startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 317 startup and SME owners, partners and employees were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis followed by AMOS-based structural path analysis in IBM SPSS analysis of moment structures (AMOS) 20.0 with maximum likelihood estimation. Specific indirect effects were assessed using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples and 95% confidence intervals. Findings All three GenAI dimensions were positively associated with entrepreneurial innovation, with knowledge modelling showing the largest reported association. Entrepreneurial innovation was positively associated with performance and success, and all six specific indirect associations were significant. The largest reported indirect associations were observed for knowledge modelling. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, single-source design supports associations rather than causal claims. Practical implications Entrepreneurs should prioritise knowledge-related practices, verification of AI-generated information and human judgement rather than treating tool use alone as evidence of innovation. Policy and support programmes should develop these practices alongside access to GenAI tools. Originality/value The study distinguishes GenAI capability, application and knowledge modelling within one entrepreneurial model and examines entrepreneurial innovation as a mediating knowledge-conversion pathway linking these dimensions with performance and success.

A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.

Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence (AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies. Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

As digital technologies become increasingly embedded in organizational processes, understanding the determinants of continued technology usage, particularly in AI-augmented digital workplaces, is essential for optimizing employee engagement and performance. This study evaluates continuance intentions in AI-augmented remote work systems by extending the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) with constructs such as perceived enjoyment, trust in technology, self-efficacy, and user satisfaction. Using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) on data from 348 experienced users of digital work platforms, our analysis reveals that trust and perceived enjoyment significantly influence satisfaction, which in turn drives continued usage intentions. Notably, the dynamics of remote work technology adoption diverge from prior information systems continuance models, with enjoyment and psychological assurance playing more prominent roles than traditionally modeled constructs like utility alone. These findings highlight the evolving expectations of knowledge workers in AI-enabled work environments, where user-centric design, intelligent automation, and trustworthy system behaviors are paramount. The study offers actionable insights for system designers and digital transformation leaders seeking to sustain user engagement in an increasingly hybrid and AI-integrated workplace. The results provide important implications for organizations designing or deploying digital collaboration tools.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69\% and 58.67\% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.

Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice.

Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates much of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning, yet adoption has outpaced theory. The tension is whether AI scaffolding relieves cognitive burden or performs the self-regulatory work autonomy requires, and implementation varies too widely for a single average to describe. Objectives. This review estimates the pooled effect of AI scaffolding on STEM achievement and self-regulated learning, tests whether technological paradigm moderates that effect, and asks whether the literature can evaluate learning after support is withdrawn. Methods. Under PRISMA 2020, four platforms searched in October 2026 (spanning 2021–2026) yielded 21,819 records; 13,786 unique records were dual-screened into an 83-record corpus, then 41 extracted cohorts. Each contributes one harmonised contrast (k = 29; N = 3,709), so within-study dependence is structurally absent. Effects were pooled by two-level random-effects meta-analysis fitted with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Results. The pooled effect was Hedges g = 0.8045 (95% CI [0.5469, 1.0621]), with τ² = 0.4410 and I² = 92.78%. The 95% prediction interval [−0.5846, 2.1936] spans zero, and no moderator reached significance. Notably, 27 of 29 cohorts (93.1%) never withdrew support, and none measured unassisted performance after removal. Conclusions. AI scaffolding yields a large but implementation-dependent gain, consistent with extraneous-load offloading rather than cognitive substitution. The decisive finding is the shape of the evidence base: the field measured a human-AI system in assembly and stayed silent on the competence of the human alone. We name this evidentiary void the Autonomy Gap. Keywords: artificial intelligence; self-regulated learning; STEM education; scaffolding fading; cognitive load theory; transfer of responsibility; meta-analysis; evidence synthesis
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

Large language model agents operating within tool-enabled pipelines create opportunities for untrusted content to influence consequential actions. This note introduces semantic privilege collapse as an architectural failure condition in which task data or insufficiently authorized instructions are promoted into effective action authority through model interpretation. The term does not claim discovery of a wholly new vulnerability: it synthesizes the confused-deputy problem, prompt-injection risks, capability-oriented control, and modern agentic authorization requirements. Drawing on OWASP’s 2025 LLM Top 10, OWASP agent-security guidance, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Simon Willison’s Dual LLM pattern, and Google DeepMind’s CaMeL research, the note distinguishes behavioral resistance to prompt injection from independently enforced execution authorization. It further distinguishes a principal’s standing permissions from task-specific authority and action-specific approval. The central argument is that semantic interpretation is not authorization evidence: protected operations require complete mediation through controls that validate identity, scope, policy, and required approvals independently of model-generated assertions. The analysis recognizes that malicious actions can remain policy-permitted when enforced policies are broader than the intended task. A reference security stack, properties of effective execution authorization, and proposed evaluation criteria are held in a restricted companion edition.

This paper presents a process-level simulation of employment impacts from artificial intelligence and automation in Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) sector. Using a representative 1,500-worker factory calibrated to recent empirical evidence, three scenarios are modelled: partial automation reflecting current observed trends (approximately 34 per cent reduction), advanced automation combined with AI applications (approximately 58 per cent reduction), and a near-full theoretical maximum (approximately 75 per cent reduction). Results indicate that helpers and lower-skilled operators bear the largest absolute and relative losses, with women accounting for roughly two-thirds of displaced workers across scenarios. Scaling the advanced scenario to sector level produces job losses on the order of 2.3 million, consistent in magnitude with independent forward projections. Technical constraints on fully autonomous sewing of complex garments, combined with potential output growth and new technical roles, moderate absolute employment decline. The findings underscore the urgency of just-transition policies, targeted reskilling, and product upgrading for Bangladesh's largest export industry. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. documents.abstract: We present a generator of Thai klon pad verse, one stanza from a short topic, and evaluate it against human verse on held-out topics. The generator is a masked language model initialised from WangchanBERTa over a fixed canvas with two layers: a sound layer of pronounced syllables, where rhyme, tone and syllable count are enforced as hard masks, and a word layer of whole words, so that no word is cut into written pieces. Decoding commits one cell at a time and samples at temperature 0.4; one sample is drawn per topic, with no selection, reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics never used in development, judged by three independent runs of a frozen LLM judge in the same pools as the human stanzas from which the topics were written, 70.5% of the generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness of all four lines and topic alignment together, against 76.9% for the human stanzas (difference -6.4 points, 95% CI [-19.2, +6.4]). Cleanness is level with human (85.9% vs. 87.2%), and the stanzas pass form and cleanness together slightly more often than the human ones (+3.8 points, [-6.4, +14.1]); the difference lies in alignment (84.6% vs. 91.0%), on topics that were written from the human stanzas. The low temperature matters: at higher temperatures the same model passes clearly fewer of the same topics, because lexical errors lie in the model's lower-probability choices; sharpening the sampling distribution removes most of them, at a cost in vocabulary (7.5% rare words against 16.5% in the human stanzas) and diversity. The pre-registered target, all-three within 5 points of human, is missed by 1.4 points. KlonSuphap-LM, the only public klon pad generator we know of, passes none of the 78 held-out topics when judged in separate pools together with the method's and the human stanzas (form 19.2%, cleanness 3.8%).

Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) is used in wildlife monitoring to reduce communication demand, support decision-making, and enable energy-aware operation, yet embedded inference alone does not establish whether a system can sustain useful service after installation. This scoping review searched four bibliographic databases through 5 August 2026 and complemented these searches with studies identified from prior work on the topic, identifying 41 eligible English-language papers published from 2021 onward on camera-primary intelligent wildlife systems. The review aimed to assess operational maturity, field-validated operational role, energy evidence, and operational continuity. Full texts were charted and analyzed across sensing, decision-making, communication, response, energy, and continuity. Post-installation evidence exposed triggering, environmental, connectivity, maintenance, and energy-supply constraints not established through non-field evaluation. Field-validated alert delivery did not extend to quantitative validation linking human action to mitigation outcomes, while field activation of physical intervention alone did not establish behavioral or management effectiveness. Energy evidence was even more limited, with limited direct operational electrical measurement, rare main-state characterization, and no complete lifetime energy budget evidence. By separating architectural capability from the evidence supporting its operational realization, the review provides a systems-level basis for interpreting how far reported functions are actually validated. Across the corpus, optimization often shifts constraints among computation, triggering, communication, energy supply, and availability rather than eliminating them. Wildlife Edge AI should therefore be evaluated as a complete field system under application-relevant conditions.

Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. Each probe contains a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control. The task is reframed from direct plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation. Social-media expressions are divided into stylistic packaging, which preserves semantic polarity, and sarcastic packaging, which reverses surface polarity. Six Chinese-capable large language models are evaluated through paired differences measuring identity bias, stylistic packaging, and sarcasm shift. All models show significant identity-bias effects; five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects; and sarcasm shifts display a clear cross-model gradient. These findings demonstrate that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation and that lower scores under sarcasm should not be interpreted directly as bias mitigation. The proposed paired design offers a measurement approach for Chinese social-media contexts while also revealing the construct boundary and prompt sensitivity of social consensus estimation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer ( B = 4.05, SE = 1.58, Wald 95% CI [0.94, 7.15], p = .011; sensitivity p = .034; Hedges’ g = 0.52). Class-clustered analyses found no Holm-adjusted difference on any Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscale; Perceived Choice had the largest positive estimate ( B = 0.27, cluster-adjusted SE = 0.12, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.55], p = .061, pHolm = .306; Hedges’ g = 0.38). The Condition × Pretest interaction was nonsignificant ( B = −0.109, SE = 0.125, 95% CI [-0.354, 0.137], p = .385). Descriptive coding of 101 matched responses showed different distributions of expected and planned AI-use orientations; no inferential transition test was conducted. Findings provide preliminary evidence concerning the bundled intervention but do not isolate component contributions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Foundation models (FM) have transformed computational pathology but remain computationally prohibitive for clinical deployment due to their massive parameter counts and high-magnification processing requirements. Here, we introduce XMAG, a lightweight FM developed through cross-magnification distillation that transfers knowledge from a state-of-the-art 20x magnification teacher to an efficient 5x magnification student architecture. XMAG employs a compact backbone and operates entirely at 5x, requiring 11.3 times fewer patches per whole slide image (WSI) compared to existing approaches. Our novel distillation framework incorporates dual-level knowledge transfer, aligning both global image representations and local spatial features across magnification levels through carefully designed projection heads and spatial token mapping. We trained XMAG on 3.49 million images curated from publicly available datasets and evaluated performance across seven clinically relevant histopathology analysis tasks spanning multiple cancer types. Across four WSI-level classification tasks, XMAG achieved an average AUC within 1% of substantially larger foundation models while delivering up to 29.5-fold faster encoder-level processing, corresponding to an encoder throughput of 8.8 WSIs per minute in a controlled patch-encoding benchmark. We also found that performance differences remained task-dependent, with larger gaps observed for fine-grained tasks such as ISUP grading and patch-level phenotyping. We further explore end-to-end XMAG training as a direction for task-specific adaptation of the compact model. These results suggest that cross-magnification distillation is a promising strategy for developing efficient low-magnification pathology foundation models and may support more scalable WSI analysis in computationally constrained research and translational settings.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, is transforming computer-assisted learning and teaching in higher education. This study investigates how ChatGPT can support learning by reducing cognitive load, with particular emphasis on the roles of user technological confidence and affective trust in artificial intelligence within the framework of Cognitive Load Theory. The study employs quantitative analysis based on data from 12,085 respondents across 135 countries, including undergraduate and postgraduate students and academic researchers. The data were analyzed using a PLS-SEM approach implemented in SmartPLS 4.0 with bootstrapping procedures. The results indicate that ChatGPT use is associated with reduced cognitive load and increased user technological confidence. User technological confidence mediates this relationship, while affective trust in AI acts as a moderating factor. A constraining effect was observed, whereby very high levels of trust in AI are associated with more passive interaction with the technology, weakening the overall effect of cognitive load reduction. These findings contribute to a better understanding of how large language models can be effectively and responsibly integrated into higher education, demonstrating that successful human–AI collaboration depends not only on the availability of AI tools but also on fostering appropriate technological confidence and balanced trust to achieve meaningful learning outcomes.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

The fast increase in artificial intelligence (AI) in vital points in society has created significant governance issues at the interface of environmental sustainability and legal responsibility. Although there is a rich literature on AI ethics, technical safety, and standalone regulatory compliance, a cohesive theoretical framework that encompasses both legal compliance and environmental responsibility conditions under one governance framework have not existed yet, seemingly conspicuously in the literature. The review thus poses the question of how legal compliance requirements and environmental accountability requirements for AI systems can be incorporated in one, theoretically coherent governance architecture, and what are the structural gaps in existing regulatory instruments in this context? This gap is filled in this paper, by introducing the Sustainable AI Governance Framework (SAGF) a conceptual model, three pillars in theory which integrates regulatory coherence, environmental accountability and legal compliance architecture. A systematic conceptual review of studies published in the period 2021–2025 and indexed in Scopus, WoS and PubMed (search on 3–10 March 2026) was carried out after PRISMA 2020. For empirical studies, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool was used to assess the quality of the studies and for doctrinal and conceptual studies, a five-item checklist was used. To develop the SAGF, 58 articles in sustainability science, environmental law, governance theory and AI regulation were selected fulfilling the inclusion criteria. The article outlines seven key global regulatory tools, seven research gaps (six corpus-derived and one framework-level), and presents a policy roadmap plan that includes mandatory carbon disclosures by AI, legal harmonization across jurisdictions, and tiered organizational standards of compliance. The results have shown that current regulatory frameworks are methodically ineffective in uniting environmental and legal aspects of AI regulation and expose structural gaps, which are inadequately addressed by technical norms and soft-law tools. The paper adds a theoretically sound and practically feasible model to help legislators, regulatory bodies, AI creators, and legal professionals negotiating the twin demands of both sustainable and legally responsible AI use on a globally scale.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The sustainability of global maritime supply chains ultimately depends on the safety of frontline port workers, yet high-risk, multi-stakeholder port operations continue to face persistent occupational hazards that threaten this goal. Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems (OHSMS) serve as a core governance tool for sustainable safety management, but their effectiveness depends not on formal existence alone, but on workers’ cognitive recognition and cultural internalization, particularly under South Korea’s Serious Accidents Punishment Act. This study examined how OHSMS perception is related to safety performance (SP) among port workers, testing the parallel and serial mediating roles of Serious Accident Response Capability (SARC) and Safety Culture (SC) as pathways toward socially sustainable safety outcomes. Cross-sectional survey data from 432 South Korean port workers were analyzed using structural equation modeling. OHSMS perception was positively associated with both SARC and SC, and SC showed the strongest direct association with SP. In the main model, the direct paths from OHSMS and SARC to SP were non-significant, consistent with indirect-only mediation through SC, and the serial pathway (OHSMS → SARC → SC → SP) was significant; however, the SARC → SP path became significant in a common method sensitivity analysis. These cross-sectional results represent associations rather than causal effects. The findings suggest that safety performance in the port sector is associated less with formal regulatory compliance alone than with the internalization of safety practices in a shared safety culture, which is relevant to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being).
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
keywords: occupational health and safety management system

documents.abstract: Given current educational trends, it is necessary to move beyond fragmented curricular approaches and promote competencies for understanding interrelationships, feedback loops, complex sociotechnical problems, technical communication, and decision-making. These capabilities must be incorporated across the curriculum through learning outcomes, projects, simulations, authentic assessment, and interdisciplinary integration. This exploratory quantitative curriculum document analysis examined 15 official course syllabi from the first educational cycle of a nationally standardized Mechatronics Engineering curriculum implemented across 130 institutions within the Mexican Technological and Polytechnic Universities subsystem. Each syllabus constituted one documentary unit of analysis (n = 15) and was coded using a 13-item ordinal rubric covering six curricular dimensions. The rubric provided initial evidence of content validity (CVI = 0.92) and sample-specific internal reliability (α = 0.888). Systemic Strategies, Interdisciplinarity, and Assessment showed strong positive associations (ρ = 0.822–0.901). Exploratory factor analysis produced a preliminary one-factor solution that accounted for 53.40% of the variance, whereas the exploratory regression showed that Systemic Strategies was the largest conditional correlate of Assessment. Given the sample size, these findings should not be interpreted as confirmation of a stable measurement structure or predictive structural model. The results highlight preliminary patterns within the intended curriculum and identify opportunities to strengthen the documented integration of communicative literacy, complex assessment, and curricular progression. Larger independent document sets and evidence from enacted and attained curricula are needed.

The growth of digital technology and artificial intelligence has pushed companies to handle their employees in a more adaptable and data-based way. Talent Intelligence has become a way to combine worker data, technology, analysis, and people factors to help make better decisions in human resources. This study looks at how Talent Intelligence is used in managing people, what role it plays in finding and boosting employee skills, how technology that uses data affects this process, and what things help or stop organizations from using it effectively today. This study uses a Systematic Literature Review method, which includes steps like searching for sources, screening them, selecting the most relevant ones, and then analyzing the content to find themes and patterns. The results show that Talent Intelligence helps companies find out what each person is good at, understand their skills, help them grow and stay with the company, and plan for future work needs by using data from employees, analyzing people data, and applying artificial intelligence. How well it works depends on the quality of the data, the ability to analyze it, how ready the organization is for digital tools, the rules in place to manage it, and the role people play in using it. The main difficulties are biased algorithms, keeping personal information safe, and how technology can't fully understand human feelings and situations. Talent Intelligence connects technology with talent growth to make organizations more flexible and prepared.

Digital transformation has changed the way organizations manage human resources, including in the areas of acquiring, developing, retaining, and mobilizing talent. In this context, talent mobility is no longer limited to employee transfers but also encompasses career mobility, knowledge transfer, competency development, and the adaptation of talent to the organization’s increasingly dynamic needs. This study aims to analyze the development of research on talent mobility within the digital ecosystem and to identify patterns of findings, methodological approaches, and key themes emerging in the literature. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach, involving a systematic process of literature identification, selection, extraction, and synthesis based on predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria.
